knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.align = "center",
                      dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)

A transition network is a first-order Markov model: the probability of the
next code is assumed to depend only on the current code, not on the codes
before it. The assumption reduces a session to a square matrix of
transition probabilities and makes the whole network analysis possible
(Saqr et al., 2025), but it is an empirical claim about the data. When the next move of a programmer
depends on the last two exchanges with the assistant rather than on the
last one, a first-order network averages over that memory and represents
the process as more random than it is.

The Markov-order test fits Markov models of increasing order to the session
sequences and tests whether each step up in order improves the fit more than
expected under the lower order. The likelihood-ratio statistic of each step
is judged against a permutation null, and the information criteria AIC and
BIC are reported for every order. In a heterogeneous network the question
has a second dimension. The order of the combined sequence describes the
joint human-AI process, while the order of each actor's own events
describes that actor's process. When the combined process needs a higher
order than either actor alone, the memory lies in the coupling between the
actors, in how a reply depends on the exchange that led to it.

```{r package}
library(htna)
```

## Data

The test is applied to three sets of sequences from the 429 vibe-coding
sessions.

- **Human events**: `human_simplified`, the human codes of each session in
  their order (six codes).
- **AI events**: `ai_simplified`, the AI codes of each session in their
  order (six codes).
- **Combined**: `human_ai`, the interleaved human and AI events of each
  session, as stored on the htna network (twelve codes).

All three tables have the session in `session_id`, the code in `code` and
the order in `order_in_session`. The per-actor sequences are single-actor
networks, built with `Nestimate::build_network()`; the combined sequence is
the htna network.

```{r data}
data(human_ai, human_simplified, ai_simplified)
human_net <- Nestimate::build_network(human_simplified, method = "relative",
                                      action = "code", session = "session_id",
                                      order = "order_in_session")
ai_net <- Nestimate::build_network(ai_simplified, method = "relative",
                                   action = "code", session = "session_id",
                                   order = "order_in_session")
net <- build_htna(human_ai, actor_type = "actor_type")
```

## Does the human's next move depend on more than the current one?

`markov_order_test_htna()` tests orders 1 to `max_order` in turn. Order 0
is the model in which codes occur independently of what came before. With
`n_perm = 200`, the smallest attainable p-value is 1/201 = 0.00498.

```{r human}
mo_human <- markov_order_test_htna(human_net, max_order = 4L, n_perm = 200L,
                                   seed = 1L)
mo_human
```

The test uses 425 of the human sequences (and, below, 425 AI and 428
combined sequences), with 10,792 human events. For the human events every
step up to order 4 is significant under the
permutation test, so the selected order saturates at the largest order
tested. The information criteria disagree with the test: AIC prefers order
2 and BIC order 1. The reason is in the degrees of freedom: the step from
order 3 to order 4 adds 4,111 parameters for 10,792 observations, so the
higher-order tables are sparse and the gain in likelihood is bought with
a large number of rarely observed contexts.

## Does the AI's next move depend on more than the current one?

The same test on the AI events is directly comparable, since it uses the
same orders, permutations and seed.

```{r ai}
mo_ai <- markov_order_test_htna(ai_net, max_order = 4L, n_perm = 200L,
                                seed = 1L)
mo_ai
```

For the AI events the steps up to order 3 are significant and the step to
order 4 is not (p = 0.194), so the permutation test selects order 3. Both
AIC and BIC prefer order 1. The AI's sequence of its own moves therefore
carries less memory than the human's.

## Does the joint process depend on more than the current move?

The combined test treats the interleaved sequence as one process over the
twelve codes. Dependence in this view can come from within-actor memory or
from the coupling between actors that the per-actor tests cannot see.

```{r combined}
mo_combined <- markov_order_test_htna(net, max_order = 4L, n_perm = 200L,
                                      seed = 1L)
mo_combined
```

Every step is significant under the permutation test (order 4 selected),
AIC prefers order 2 and BIC order 1. At order 4 the model has 16,296
degrees of freedom for 19,346 observations; the asymptotic p-value of that
step is 1.00 while the permutation p-value is 0.00498, which shows how far
the chi-square approximation fails on such sparse tables and why the
permutation test is used.

```{r combined-plot}
plot(mo_combined)
```

The plot shows the log-likelihood and the information criteria of each
order beside the permutation null distributions of the test statistics.
In the table, the log-likelihood keeps rising with the order, while BIC is
lowest at order 1 (75,955) and AIC at order 2 (70,683).

## What do the three tests say together?

| Sequences | Permutation | AIC | BIC |
|---|---|---|---|
| Human events | 4 (largest tested) | 2 | 1 |
| AI events | 3 | 1 | 1 |
| Combined | 4 (largest tested) | 2 | 1 |

None of the three sets is first-order under the permutation test, and the
human events and the combined process show memory beyond the largest order
tested. The penalized criteria favor a first- or second-order model in
every case, because the higher-order contexts are too many to be estimated
from about 430 sequences. The first-order heterogeneous network is therefore a
simplification of these data: it describes the aggregate transitions
between codes and actors faithfully, but it does not represent how a move
depends on the exchange before it. Claims about turn-taking that span
several moves, such as a human request, an AI plan and the following AI
execution, are better examined with the patterns of the [Sequences and
patterns](sequences-and-patterns.html) guide than with single edges.

When the selected order equals `max_order`, the test has not found the
order of the process, only a lower bound for it; `max_order` can be raised
at the cost of still sparser tables. The number of parameters at order
*k* grows roughly as the number of codes to the power *k* + 1.

## What if the first-order assumption is rejected?

The first-order network remains a valid description of transition
frequencies; what changes is the claim it can support. Three alternatives
address different reasons for the rejection.

| Reason for the rejection | Model |
|---|---|
| The next code depends on several preceding codes | Higher-order networks: `Nestimate::build_hon()`, `Nestimate::build_honem()`, `Nestimate::build_hypa()`, `Nestimate::build_mogen()` |
| The sessions mix several first-order processes, which together look higher-order | A mixture of Markov chains, `Nestimate::cluster_mmm()`; see [Clustering inputs](clustering.html) |
| Influence fades over several steps rather than ending after one | `build_htna(..., method = "attention")` |

The actor partition is not carried by higher-order networks, whose nodes are
contexts of several codes rather than single codes; a mixture of Markov
chains keeps the partition and returns one heterogeneous network per
cluster.
